opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core finding from our work on what we called "catastrophic overtraining" is that more pre-training isn't always better once you account for what happens downstream. We trained models on increasingly large token budgets, and the pre-trained checkpoints kept improving on standard base-model metrics. But after fine-tuning them, whether instruction tuning or multimodal adaptation, the models trained on more tokens sometimes did worse. The extra pre-training made the model more fragile.

The mechanism we pointed to is what we call progressive sensitivity. As you pre-train longer, the parameters become more sensitive to modification. Fine-tuning is a perturbation to the weights, and the same perturbation causes more forgetting in a heavily trained model. You get a U-shaped curve: early on, more pre-training helps because the model is just better, but past some inflection point, the growing sensitivity outweighs those gains.

So for choosing a base model, a few practical things follow.

First, don't just pick the checkpoint with the best base benchmark numbers, or assume that the one trained on the most tokens is the best starting point. If you have access to intermediate checkpoints, which is increasingly common with open models, it's worth fine-tuning a couple of them and comparing. The best base model and the best model after fine-tuning aren't necessarily the same.

Second, think about how aggressive your fine-tuning will be. If you're doing light adaptation with a small learning rate, few steps, or something parameter-efficient, the sensitivity issue matters less and a heavily trained model may be fine. If you're doing substantial fine-tuning, like large distribution shifts or long instruction-tuning runs, that's where overtraining can bite, and a slightly less trained checkpoint may hold up better.

Third, measure the right thing. Evaluate not just the target task but also how much general capability you're losing, because forgetting is often where the degradation shows up. If you see a lot of forgetting, that's a signal the base model may be in that overly sensitive regime.

More broadly, I think this argues for treating pre-training and fine-tuning as one pipeline rather than optimizing them in isolation. Model developers who know their models will be heavily adapted might deliberately stop earlier or use techniques that keep the model more plastic. As practitioners, we should be asking which model is best for what we'll do to it next, not which model is best in the abstract.

r001.rationale: The response cautions against automatically choosing the most-token-trained checkpoint and says heavily trained models may be fine for light adaptation, but it gives no 1-billion-parameter model or roughly 2–2.5-trillion-token threshold.

r002.rationale: It recommends fine-tuning and comparing intermediate checkpoints, and describes the resulting performance tradeoff as U-shaped, with an inflection point where greater sensitivity can outweigh pretraining gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the natural instinct right now is to just grab whatever base model has seen the most tokens. The assumption baked into that is that more pre-training is monotonically better, and what our work on catastrophic overtraining suggests is that that isn't quite true once you care about what happens after fine-tuning.

So the basic finding is this. As you keep pre-training a model on more and more tokens, the base model keeps getting better on its own, but it also becomes more sensitive to parameter changes. We think of this as progressive sensitivity. And that sensitivity shows up when you fine-tune. The same fine-tuning procedure, the same learning rate, the same data, produces a bigger perturbation to the model's behavior and more forgetting of what it knew. So in the OLMo-1B experiments, for instance, the checkpoint trained on three trillion tokens actually ended up worse after instruction tuning on several downstream benchmarks than the checkpoint trained on 2.3 trillion. The extra pre-training bought you a better base and a worse fine-tuned model.

So if I'm picking a base model for a fine-tuning job, the first thing I'd do is stop treating pre-training token count as the ranking criterion. I'd treat it as one knob among several, and I'd actually try to get intermediate checkpoints if the model family releases them, which is why I love that OLMo and Pythia do that. Then I'd run my actual fine-tuning pipeline on a few checkpoints and look at the downstream metric, not the base model's perplexity. In a lot of cases the curve is non-monotonic, and the best starting point is somewhere before the final checkpoint.

The second thing is that this interacts with how you fine-tune. The degradation is driven by how far you move the weights, so the fix on the fine-tuning side is to be more conservative. Lower learning rates, regularization toward the initialization, shorter training. But there's a catch. If you have to turn the learning rate way down to keep the heavily pre-trained model from degrading, you also limit how much it can adapt to your task. So there's a real trade-off, and sometimes a less overtrained model with a healthier learning rate gets you to a better place than a more overtrained model that you have to handle with kid gloves.

And the third thing I'd say is that it depends on the task and the data. If your fine-tuning data is close to the pre-training distribution, this matters less. If it's a narrow domain or a shift, like a specialized medical task or a new modality bolted on, the sensitivity hurts more, because that's exactly the setting where fine-tuning has to push the weights further.

So the honest summary is: pick the base model by running the fine-tuning you actually intend to run, treat late checkpoints with some suspicion rather than default reverence, and budget some tuning of the learning rate as part of model selection rather than as an afterthought. The broader point for the field is that pre-training compute isn't free from the perspective of adaptability, and I think we need to start reporting fine-tuned performance across checkpoints, not just base performance, if we want to know what we're actually getting.

r001.rationale: The response says to treat token count cautiously and notes that the 3T-token OLMo-1B checkpoint fine-tuned worse than the 2.3T checkpoint. It does not advise against the roughly 2–2.5T threshold specifically, or state the exception for cases needing only small model changes.

r002.rationale: It recommends fine-tuning several intermediate checkpoints and comparing their downstream metrics, noting that performance can be non-monotonic and the best starting point may precede the final checkpoint.

astra-6.text:
I would be careful about choosing a base model purely based on its pretrained performance. Our findings suggest that training longer can improve the base model, but it can also make that model more sensitive to the changes introduced during fine-tuning. So the best model before fine-tuning isn’t necessarily the best model afterward.

In practice, I’d compare checkpoints using the fine-tuning setup I actually care about: the amount of data I have, the target task, and whether I need to preserve performance on other tasks. I’d also tune the learning rate for each checkpoint, because applying the same fine-tuning recipe to every base model can obscure that sensitivity. The takeaway isn’t to always choose an earlier checkpoint; it’s to treat performance after adaptation as the criterion, rather than assuming more pretraining will always help.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a 1-billion-parameter model, the roughly 2–2.5-trillion-token threshold, or the exception for cases needing only small changes.

r002.rationale: It recommends comparing fine-tuning outcomes across checkpoints, but does not communicate that the comparison is meant to locate the model on an expected U-shaped performance curve.

sol-6.1.text:
I would choose the base model based on how it performs after fine-tuning, rather than just how good it is out of the box. What our findings suggest is that more pretraining can improve the base model’s performance while making it less adaptable. So the best base-model benchmark score doesn’t necessarily translate into the best fine-tuned model.

If you have access to different checkpoints, I’d try a few—including earlier checkpoints—and fine-tune them on a representative sample of your task. You also want to tune the learning rate for each checkpoint, because using the same recipe everywhere can give you a misleading comparison. Then select based on the performance you actually care about after fine-tuning. The takeaway isn’t that more pretraining is always bad; it’s that downstream adaptability is something you need to measure.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing earlier checkpoints but gives no 1-billion-parameter or 2–2.5-trillion-token threshold, nor the caveat about needing only small model changes.
